commenti.body:
It's been said before that it's wrong to watch a movie in the sense that you are "figuring it out" as your prime interaction with it.  There's a lot of focus on twist endings and people seem to want a full explanation of everything.  I enjoy learning as I go but from subtle clues.  And there's nothing wrong with a little mystery.  I like open-ended endings.  The end of History of Violence always resonated with me as it's ambigious and I and the person I watched it with had totally different takes on the ending.

Anyways I'm rambling here hopefully I touched on some points that are on topic with your observations.

I definitely find and excess of exposition in tentpole movies these days. And to make matters worse, most of it is just mcguffin gobbledygook. 

I can tell you as a television writer that over-explaining is now mandated by networks who acknowledge and embrace the fact that people are usually scrolling their phones, cooking, or doing laundry while they watch. So there is an amount of exposition I feel is necessary for an audience and I am usually noted into doubling that amount. 

Televisions are referred to as ‘second screens’, with your phone or tablet being the first.

I do think there are certain plot elements that major motion pictures insist on beating their audience over the head with importance to make sure everyone gets it before the mcguffin itself goes in to action.

To this end, I will defend Christopher Nolan's work for its lack of handholding and insisting you watch the film a second time if you missed out on a key plot point being revealed during the first watch.

Too often movies are made now for people who are fooling around on their phone during the film events instead of being made for an audience dedicated to viewing the events unfold on screen.

Now, to be fair, not every movie does this, but it does seem to be a big feature in larger budget films to the point I imagine some producer who barely paid attention to the screening itself complaining that it was hard to follow forcing some reshoots and added scenes to clarify what was already explained earlier in the film.

To answer the question in short: Absolutely.

I think it has to do with the attention spans of audiences; these days it seems like if a movie doesn't reveal everything about itself in the first 10 minutes, then there's a large segment of the audience that will lose interest.

Even great veteran filmmakers have fallen into this trap.  David Fincher's latest work The Killer is weighed down by an unnecessary voiceover that over-explains its main character; the film would have been much more effective without it.  Of course, this is not 100% the rule for every film - this year alone we've had both Killers of the Flower Moon and Oppenheimer, which are very deliberate in their pacing and all the better for it.
It feels like modern producers are terrified of their audience having to watch the film a second time to "get it" so they do everything in their power to avoid that.

Over explanation in narrative cinema is the one aspect of the reification of our collective existential drive for explanation and understanding. It’s also the long legacy of Freudian psychology over against subsequent generations’ discoveries that humans don’t ever really consciously know why we’re doing what we do. And certainly can’t trace it back to one primal scene or traumatic origin story. We think knowing in this or that smaller instance will help us grapple with all the big stuff that we still don’t know and can’t control. We’re not comfortable with uncertainty. We don’t know enough to know that knowing is not enough.
Yes, adding the subplot where Salieri sexually blackmails Konstanze adds nothing to the rest of the story, apart from making Salieri look creepy and showing us Konstanze’s breasts in their entirety.

Something I've noticed recently is that Genre is no longer considered a pre-explanation for certain things. It seems that Genre blending has been taken to such a degree that it doesn't mean anything anymore and a lot of people just ignore it completely.

A bizarre example: During a movie club discussion of The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover, someone complained that he didn't buy into the romance between the Wife and her Lover. They just... didn't find it convincing enough to justify the plot of the movie. They were right in the sense that the movie didn't dwell on the character motivations -- it started the movie with the motivations presented by the setting and genre.

Therefore, movies can't just fall back to "It's a Sci-Fi movie; it's okay to not explain why the characters are exploring the planet. They're explorers. It's in the premise because of genre." Or, "It's an Action movie; it's okay to not explain why the protag is a stoic badass. He just is. That's the genre."

And this leads to movies attempting to justify everything to the audience. We apparently need to know the dark past of the stoic action hero. Or _why_ the slasher villain is trying to kill a house full of skimpy-clothed sorority members.

It reminds me of a teacher's dilemma who's trying to teach a class of children with very different levels of understanding. It might seem self-evident that the teacher should adjust the tempo to the "slowest" kid, and repeat the explanation until finally they also understand it. But by doing so, the teacher will lose the attention of most of his students who understood the concept immediately. A good teacher will find a way to entertain both groups with different tasks, or she will make sure that the additional explanations will illuminate different facets of the same concept, furthering the understanding of both the slower and the faster kids.

So, how would that look like in the movies? (This is not one of those rhetorical questions you find in bad articles; I'm really asking myself and I'm not sure what the answer is.)

Often I find myself wishing for a Star Wars scroll that would just handle the exposition in two minutes of reading replacing one hour of drab expositional dialogue. And in some movies (for instance the last Mission Impossible) my answer would be to just simplify the plot. We all know the whole thing is an excuse for Tom Cruise to jump off a cliff, so why not have a robo-elephant chase after him instead of all that double agent dubious morality artificial intelligence ballyhoo. The dumb viewers are frustrated because they don't grasp it, the smart viewers are frustrated because it's some blown-up bullshit. Both will be happy with a robo-elephant.

They definitely do. I think many people don’t understand what a plot hole is anymore because of it. They call any instance of characters not knowing the full story as a plot hole. That’s just an incorrect way to view things.

The more distressing aspect of movies now to me is that there are a lot fewer films made now with intentional calm silence shared between characters.

I haven't seen Amadeus director's cut, So I can't really comment on that but I've rarely felt that movies "explain too much". There are times where I've felt the explanation was done in a lazy manner more so than it being unnecessary. 

>The need to build franchises means ample opportunity to fill in backstories, which is one of the reasons I think over-explanation seems to be on the rise these days. 

Well, then your issue should be with cinematic universes/franchises with a lot of world building no? If you're going to make a film like Dune where you have multiple factions, sci-fi tech specific to this story, extensive in-universe history that drives the current year events in the plot you're going to need a lot of exposition. 

There are, of course, people who take it too far and demand an explanation for each and every aspect of the lore so they can fill in wiki articles. Those types should be ignored but so far I don't think movies have reached a point where autistic lore building are given more priority than the story and themes.

It seems to be a common theme nowadays. I’ve especially noticed it when discussing films with general audiences or people who casually enjoy movies. There seems to be a frustration and parallel desire to understand a film’s narrative, themes and meaning. This comes with a fair bit of criticism & weighs heavy on some people’s experience with a film. I’ve seen people dismiss brilliant works of art over a lack of understanding pertaining to the narrative. Ignoring all the other cinematic elements as if their souls purpose is narrative driven. 

As an American I genuinely wonder if our school system sets us up for this mentality. We write essay after essay discussing themes of books & breaking down the “right” and “wrong” clues to unraveling narratives in a traditional classroom setting. Some of us are fortunate enough to stray from the pack later in life & unlearn this need to understand & replace it with the desire to simply feel & experience.

For me it is a bit discouraging when I walk away from a movie & the people I’m with are only concerned with the “why” of the story. I completely understand there are different forms of cinema & a lot of people enjoy traditional plot & narrative. It’s comforting & allows us to move with the movie in an intellectual sense. But at the same time, major (American) movies seem to be becoming “over explainy” & dependents upon narrative structure.  

It’s a shame. Cinema is and always has been more than plot structure. & films drenched in exposition take away from the immersion, mystery and magic in my opinion. Of course this is dependent upon the subject & changes with every film.
Would love to hear your take on the ending of a History of Violence, or just the film itself.

For just the horror genre, I'm a huge fan of horror movies that don't explain themselves. 

The original paradigm for me is "Phantasm," which I saw in the theater, and walked out thinking how much the film was like a dream or nightmare because stuff just kind of happens for no reason. "Eraserhead" took it a step further. 

For recent films, the "V/H/S" series has a lot of segments like that, the peak being the "Cult" segment in "V/H/S/2." And I'm a big fan of the widely unpopular film "YELLOWBRICKROAD" because it makes absolutely no sense, and doesn't *try* to make sense.

I personally draw the line at "Skinamarink," but to be fair, I have yet to make it to an hour in before I give up.

IMO, they're carrying on the tradition of the surrealists like Bunuel; it's hard to argue that "Eraserhead" isn't a surrealist film. I also think it's more common in the horror genre than in other genres, at least for recent films.

I agree with you that films are overly “talky” today, one of my least directors is Greta Gerwig for this reason.

I dislike it when films condescend to their audiences in this manner. I also think it constitutes mediocre storytelling and dull art. A good storyteller learns how to convey a great deal by saying very little. Characters are more interesting by what isn’t directly revealed to us, but hidden in the shadows and layers.  

I do want to point out that director’s cuts are notoriously awful. There’s a reason why the editor cuts out additional scenes. Directors cling to their footage as if adding to a film is going to benefit their art piece. It’s usually the opposite because editing is not their forte. Editing is an art onto its own and directors don’t want to relinquish their vision to anyone. Editors are the true storytellers in filmmaking, not directors.

Anytime I try and converse with anyone under 25, I do get the vibe that they don’t understand nuance or subtly. Perhaps it’s a youth thing and needs to be acquired over time.

I think your last paragraph is the key issue. There are simultaneous demands for clear explanation but a rejection of anything that looks like "telling" rather than "showing" and a disdain for anything too much like a simple genre plot. So you get these movies with unnecessarily complex plots and attempts to tell politically/ideologically/emotionally resonant stories that are bogged down in contrived ways to "show" their plot.
Which always reminds me of Raymond Chandler who famously couldn't explain the end of The Big Sleep.

I believe this issue is more common with director's cuts in general. Overexploitation is just one of its symptoms. In many instances, the extended runtime doesn't justify its existence and dilutes a much tighter and ultimately more satisfying theatrical version. 'Apocalypse Now' is a prime example of this. Personally, one of my pet peeves is whatever Cameron Crowe did to the fantastic theatrical cut of 'Almost Famous'.

Appreciate this perspective.  My answer would've been a resounding "no" due to the ongoing production of more experimental films that even sometimes lose people and lead to hateful audience reactions due to a lack of exposition (thinking particularly of *Skinamarink*, but take your pick).  Can't really argue with that experience though - or even the fact that sometimes I do exactly what you're describing and choose perceived depth of what I'm going to watch based on whether I'm going to have another screen open or not.  It sounds exhausting to have to deal with as a writer though.

>Often I find myself wishing for a Star Wars scroll that would just handle the exposition in two minutes of reading replacing one hour of drab expositional dialogue.

My pet peeve is the contrast between the original _Alien_ and modern semi-franchise movies, _Prometheus_ and _Covenant_.

Original _Alien_ didn't explain ANYTHING.  It provided a mystery,  questions about the derelict ship, it's passenger and origin. 

These modern movies on the other hand, provide zero mystery, nothing is left unexplained.

Granted, the comparison is unfair in that sense that the series became more lore-heavy already when it became a _franchise_.

Still,  the original _Alien_ was truly "alien", an unknown entity and it's world was full of mystery.  And it was all the better for it.

Nah you’re missing the entire point of The Killer!! The voice-over is deliberately unreliable. He’s constantly wrong, constantly over-confident, constantly contradicting himself. The whole point of the movie is that this guy’s ego and self-image are always holding him back, or papering over his own emotions that he can’t admit to himself. It’s a satire! The movie *is* the voice over. Without it, it’s just a rote, mostly silent assassin-revenge flick

Honestly a lot of the problems SW super fans have with The Last Jedi is that it doesn’t explain it’s own themes and character motivations in the type of exposition dumps that are common in blockbusters (and it still explains everything a fair bit, mind you). But compared to the usual blockbuster fare, TLJ makes you work for it, at least a bit.

Yeah there are still lots of arthouse movies and some prestige TV series that work on the assumption of an attentive and intuitive audience, but most of my work has been in network procedurals, which have reached descriptive audio levels of exposition. It's practically radio drama at this point. But writing for TV has always been about compromises and constraints so we roll with it, and it's still a pretty fun job when you're working with a good team.

>She already is upset, obviously, about the damage composing the Requiem is doing

Not just that, but I like to think over the years, she'd figured out Salieri as a dangerous phony. At the very least, even without the sexual proposition scene, she'll have remembered that he coldly walked out on her when she asked him for help in finding Mozart some teaching jobs. Maybe he made amends after ("I was so overwhelmed with ecstasy from you husband's music that I needed a moment!"), but still, she probably would've been on alert. And as a testament to her intelligence, she saw what nobody else, especially Mozart, saw. Maybe she even tried telling Mozart but he was too proud and stubborn to think that Salieri could feel anything else towards him besides admiration and respect (even though Mozart was happy to publicly disparage Salieri).

That's a lot of filling in the blanks, but that's what made the movie so intriguing and mysterious. But nah, now the supposed canon version says that Salieri tried to Weinstein her, so that's why Stanzi hates him. Intrigue gone.

There was a scene in the latest Mission Impossible where a chorus of intelligence directors are all standing or sitting (one is even sprawled out lounging) in a room as they proceed to explain to the director of NSA what’s going on. The director of NSA seems totally out of the loop as each character gives their lines from what sounds like one speech. It felt like watching a Greek chorus in a stage play setting the scene for the drama ahead. Overall because it was done so tastefully, I thought it worked and had enough style to be worth it. But it made no rational sense for the director of the NSA to be so clueless.

I teach Media at a high school and its become noticeably more difficult to teach genre to young students because they have fewer opportunities to be exposed to the codes and conventions of multiple different genres. 

I attribute this mostly to the the rise of the internet, particularly with streaming services, have disrupted traditional media (i.e. network television, theatres, video stores, etc.). These mediums are certainly worthy of criticism, but because they were in charge of curation, the audience had no choice of what was available. In hindsight, this gave the audience the potential to watch something they otherwise would never have seen. Think of the old days of channel surfing, and just sliding into the groove of a random film you thought looked interesting, even if you start watching ten minutes in. That sense of media discovery is almost lost from an entire generation.

​

Compare that to the "infinite" choice provided by streamers, and how their algorithms seek to promote and produce similar content to what the viewer is already used to. For example, I've had more than one student who almost exclusively watch anime, because why wouldn't you watch the same thing if you know you'll enjoy it. The problem with this is that the viewer potentially DOES enjoy other genres, but other than pleasure, it also denies them the potential of broadening their creative knowledge of genres across mediums.

Producers are well aware that they are creating background noise for someone while they scroll through a news feed and, as such, they repeat plot points and exposition ad nauseum. The best example I can think of this are the hundreds of documentary mini-series that Netflix produces, and how they all go for 3+ hours, for the sole reason of being on-screen for a long time. Its even worse for fiction film and television, because character moments that don't directly connect to the plot are becoming more rare. Think of the sex scene discourse, the obsession with "plot holes", Cinema Sins style viewing, and that characters can't just live in the world of the text.  
If Netflix were to make Pulp Fiction today, Vincent and Jules would probably meticulously list the reasons  of why they have to kill Brad on the drive over, rather than talk about the Royale with Cheese.
Preach! Beautifully put.

Part of the larger plague of media-illiteracy that many, many people suffer from (and, more importantly, we who do not suffer from it still suffer from having to hear the nonsense they say!)

And sometimes they're *smug* about it, too, that's quite a bit worse.

> I teach Media at a high school and its become noticeably more difficult to teach genre to young students because they have fewer opportunities to be exposed to the codes and conventions of multiple different genres. 

I had some really interesting conversations with younger folks about The Searchers and found it really hard to explain why it works so well as _a Western_. They just didn't have the same frame of reference to get why John Wayne playing such an asshole was so interesting to fans of the genre.

> Think of the old days of channel surfing, and just sliding into the groove of a random film you thought looked interesting, even if you start watching ten minutes in.

Or, more specifically, whoever held the remote got to choose and there was no escape hatch. You either sucked it up and watched some sci-fi or you gave up and read a book. As a kid I watched a _lot_ of "boring" movies but they built the foundation of how I now approach romantic dramas and film noir.

> The problem with this is that the viewer potentially DOES enjoy other genres, but other than pleasure, it also denies them the potential of broadening their creative knowledge of genres across mediums.

I agree. I see a similar problem with people who have big lists of 5/5 movies that they crunch through because everything is available on the internet. There are a lot of people who refuse to watch "bad movies" -- and they can realistically never watch one. But there are "bad movies" that you CAN enjoy and there is a special experience chatting about silly things with your friends.

That just doesn't happen the same way anymore.
Ironically, we can do now do exactly those things because of all the other Hannibal Lector inspired media...

Yeah I don't know how someone could miss it because by then end he said "stick to the plan" about 7 times and he never sticks to the plan. He constantly go against the monologue he said at the beginning.

The very first scene is him literally being like “never be distracted, never pass on a good opportunity” as he gets distracted by the sex worker and misses on several good opportunities to kill the target — followed immediately by him missing his target.

They most certainly do! I'm only 35 but as a cinema enthusiast I know what to listen for and how to watch a movie. Looking at people on YouTube react to films mostly is pure agonizing stuff as they literally don't listen properly or get what they're watching. I've literally watched people react to Titanic wondering what Cal needs with Rose. Really?! You don't understand that the mom is trying to get them into a relationship because their family is broke and marrying him will give them money?! There's literally a whole scene dedicated to telling you exactly that through a conversation that seems natural and flows and you didn't pick that up? That's just one example but going back to the Post at hand most certainly do movies over simplify things and overexplain elements of the plot and spoonfeed to the audience that otherwise would've been better suited being explained away in the background or through the story and natural development of the plot.

We need a prequel to 2001 where we see how Dave became interested in being an astronaut, and there's a post-credit sequence of HAL coming online. Bonus points if there's a version of The Blue Danube being plunked out slowly on a piano.

Your last point really speaks to me.  With complete audience choice, you're right in that there is no "realistic" way to watch a "bad movie" anymore.. If someone were to only watch certified 5-star classics or only one kind of movie, I doubt you can truly appreciate them if you have nothing "bad" to compare it to.  In addition, films that had a negative reception in the past could find it harder to be re-evaluated. Think how crucial HBO was or SBS (Australia) is to rehabilitating the reputations of so many films, because they repeatedly showed them (i.e. John Carpenter's *The Thing*).

Yes, not only is there a trend in over explaining things but, more egregiously, it's over explaining simple things. Simple plot points, simple character motivations, and simple dialogue is reemphasized. Like showing hidden video footage of a top secret research facility on a phone is considered highbrow.

However!—

> directors and writers to want to err on the side of not trusting audiences [...]

...are absolutely correct. It is painfully evident that mainstream audience skews awesomely towards very vanilla, resealable, factory farmed entertainment across all general media formats. People are attracted to these overexplained stories not because they dislike it, obviously. Even people who pretend to dislike these types of films will readily consume them ad nauseum.

So, yes, films nowadays are simplified (synthesized) to the extreme. And yes, they need to be because the audience needs and wants it like that.
God I hate that. I have such a hard time with the idea of turning something on without the intention of giving it my full attention, unless it's something I've seen a zillion times.

I've been trying to watch more older films lately and I've *really* noticed how much more they expect of the audience. If you're not paying full attention and making sure you're attuned to what the film might be implying, you'll get lost quickly.

I think it's more of a logical conclusion or consequence of over intellectualizing and scrutinizing stories that came before as a form of meta commentary, criticism, and avoiding cliches. Because the natural conclusion of a genre has already been synthesized in the past and can no longer be refined further in the minds of the audience, film writers use techniques of surprise and cheap thrills as a way to garner a "sex appeal" to their project. I think modem films are very, very, very afraid of being artistically candid/serious and deeply resents cliches and archetypal stories. Hence, the genre-bending and lurid roller coaster spectacles so popular nowadays is a kind of half attempt at proving itself as a true art form while simultaneously saying "don't take this seriously (i.e., avoid criticism.)

been watching a fuck ton of big 70s movies ive never seen lately, and i could totally feel the difference with some modern storytelling, a lot of what ive seen from the 70s dont hold your hand at all and respect the audience to find context clues or even just be ambiguous about a divisive topic. feels like the opposite of how a lot of things nowadays spoonfeed a ton and feel like they lead you into the direction of how they want you to feel about it instead of simply presenting something as is without hammering the subtext into your head

I’m the same way, but a lot of people have tv on as background noise or ‘company’, kind of ambient narrative that doesn’t ask much of them. I’d prefer a captive audience but we’ve got to write for the audience we’ve got. 

Ironically, when people are two-screening and live posting about episodes on social media while they watch, it’s a real positive for the show.

> **Imagine** how lame Silence of the Lambs would have been if we had to sit through some boring backstory of Hannibal’s or Bill’s mom being mean to him as a kid.

I haven’t seen the director’s cut of Amadeus you referred to, but some things came to mind.

Usually, when a director’s cut is released, the implication is that we’re seeing a version of the movie that’s aligned to the director’s original vision - that, for whatever reason, didn’t make it into the theatrical cut.

The theatrical cut is the result of many factors: for running time, which means more screenings, which means more money; for a less divisive and more appealing narrative, and so on. Rarely is the case where a producer will interfere because a movie is overexplaining. Most of the time, it’s because they want to make it more accessible for audiences everywhere.

Also, a director’s cut is different from an extended edition, though those terms have been used interchangeably in some occasions. The Lord of the Rings films have an extended version that includes scenes that were left in the editing room and that die-hard fans enjoyed seeing it, but Peter Jackson was perfectly satisfied with the version that hit the theaters and has publicly stated this is the version viewers should look for. I absolutely agree with him; the original cut is more focused, the narrative flows better, the additional scenes make the movies drag.

To wrap this up: a director’s cut, or an extended cut, is not necessarily the best version of the movie. If a director's cut, released after an original cut that was hugely successful and understood on its own, have no reason to oversimplify things, unless the director wants to include everything that was shot.

I disagree re: the added scenes in Amadeus.  Those scenes are not about Atwnzi; they’re about Salieri, and the depth of his internal battles with his faith, his jealousy of Mozart, and his own boundless vanity.  

Salieri has made a vow of chastity.  He intensely loves his opera singer, but would never touch her.  And he intensely loves his status as Court Composer. Losing her to Mozart’s new opera is bad enough, but losing her to Mozart himself, the creature, is unbearable.  His ego and vanity can’t handle it.  His faith is rocked to its foundations.  How could God allow such a thing to happen? 

His impulse to have sex with Stanzi in exchange for getting Mozart a job is motivated by jealousy, displaced lust, anger at God, and a desire for revenge so powerful, he’s prepared to abandon his vow of chastity.  But at the moment of opportunity, he cannot go through it.  His hatred for Mozart, and his own vanity, will not permit him to do so.  It’s a major moment of choice for him.  His vanity won’t allow him to lower himself to  tennis bow or chastity and sleep with this woman who is so clueless about Mozart’s greatness; and his rage and jealousy won’t allow him to put himself in a position where he’s obligated to get Mozart a job in exchange for sex.  He simply rejects her, and walks out on her like a piece of trash.  

Reconsider these as fantastic scenes about Salieri’s inner turmoil, despair, and anger.  Stanzi is little more than a proxy if not a bystander.
